source.title: Painless step size adaptation for SGD

record.file_problem: None; the supplied text contains the full paper, including its appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on test accuracy using a modified step-size method, but does not measure the training classification error or test any of the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The CIFAR10 results report test accuracy on a binarized, 1,000-sample subset; they do not establish training classification error. Other experiments and cited prior-work results do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study compares LIGHT activation configurations and optimizers using test accuracy and epochs to test-accuracy thresholds. It reports no training classification error, initialization comparison, deep-network degradation, batch-normalization comparison, or measured loss/curvature dynamics relative to a stability threshold. Its discussion of the edge of stability does not test V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that LIGHT's fixed growth and decline rates explicitly control the convergence/generalization trade-off, and propose that this could enable reliable, explainable architectures without overparameterization. Their empirical measures are test accuracy and epochs, so these conclusions do not establish the training-error or stability-threshold behavior named in the claim versions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a LIGHT-modified output activation to adapt the SGD step size; reports test accuracy rather than training classification error.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports differing outcomes across LIGHT configurations, datasets, network architectures, and variance conditions; these do not test the listed claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: On 1,000 sampled CIFAR-10 images with binarized labels and an 80/20 split, maximum test accuracy was 88.1%, 88.2%, 88.1%, and 90.5% for sigmoid-Adam, sigmoid-AdaGrad, sigmoid-SGD, and LIGHT-g-SGD, respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LIGHT-g-SGD achieved higher selected maximum test accuracy than these sigmoid optimizer baselines in this small binary classification experiment.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
record.problems: The reported CIFAR10 experiment uses 1,000 randomly sampled examples, binarizes labels to target class {5}, and reports test accuracy rather than training error. The supplied text gives no uncertainty estimates for these results.
record.rows_left_out: No other rows retained: synthetic and MNIST/Fashion MNIST results are test-accuracy results outside the listed claim versions; cited prior-work results are not this study's own results.

untested.parts: Training classification error in sufficiently large convolutional networks, including corrupted/random labels and the effects of size, early stopping, and regularization.
Spurious local minima in ReLU teacher-student problems and their dependence on student width.
Depth-dependent training degradation, identity shortcuts, and the stated initialization alternatives.
Initialization-dependent training speed, signal/gradient propagation, and trainable depth.
Recovery or divergence relative to an initial stability limit, curvature reduction, and sharpness tracking the stability threshold.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: References to initialization, batch normalization, and edge-of-stability findings are background discussion. The supplied text contains no additional own result testing V1–V6.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, random or corrupted labels, CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 benchmark training, model size, and early stopping.
Teacher-student local minima and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth effects on training error and residual shortcuts.
Initialization effects on training speed or trainable depth.
Training behavior around a stability limit and sharpness.
Batch normalization effects on training speed or learning-rate tolerance.
